Real `burrow-engine` failure envelopes, captured verbatim from a release build.

These are CAPTURES, not fixtures: every byte is stdout from the actual engine binary, so the
tests that load them assert against what the engine really emits rather than against a shape
someone typed out by hand (RULEBOOK section 3e).

FIRST BATCH — the four below. Captured 2026-08-08 at 10:28 local, macOS 25.5.0 (arm64), from a
`cargo build --release` of burrow-engine at e1b46b6 ("chore: untrack .DS_Store"), reporting
burrow_cli 0.1.0. That checkout had another
author's work uncommitted at the time, so every message string below was checked against
`git show HEAD:` for the file it comes from and is present at the commit as stated — the captures
are of the committed wording, not of somebody's in-flight edit.

The two `unsupported` captures needed their failure PROVOKED on macOS, where both commands
normally succeed. `sandbox-exec` does that honestly — the engine's own code takes its own error
branch because the syscall really was refused — instead of a hand-written stub pretending to.


net-unsupported.json
    sandbox-exec -p '(version 1)(allow default)
                     (deny process-exec* (literal "/usr/bin/nettop"))' \
      burrow-engine net --limit 1

    `/usr/bin/nettop` still exists, so `net::resolve_nettop` succeeds and `run_nettop` is the
    thing that fails — `cli.rs:372`'s `unsupported_envelope`, kind `unsupported`.


orphans-unsupported.json
    sandbox-exec -p '(version 1)(allow default)
                     (deny file-read* (subpath "/Applications"))' \
      burrow-engine orphans /tmp

    `orphan::enumerate_installed_apps_checked` cannot `read_dir("/Applications")`, so the
    inventory is missing rather than empty — `cli.rs:447`'s `unsupported_envelope`.


slim-check-error.json
    burrow-engine slim-check <the burrow-engine binary itself>

    A Rust-built binary is a thin Mach-O, so `macho::parse_fat` refuses it. This one goes
    through `error_envelope` (`cli.rs:499`), and the engine's OWN wording table classifies it
    `error` — which is why relaying the kind does not change this command's answer. Kept as the
    capture that proves the relay reports `error` when `error` is what the engine said, rather
    than only ever upgrading things to `unsupported`.


net-unsupported-reworded.json
    THE REGRESSION CAPTURE. Same `net` invocation and sandbox as above, but against an engine
    whose message was reworded — `"per-app network unavailable: "` replaced with the same-length
    `"per-app network is off here: "`, patched into a COPY of the release binary and ad-hoc
    re-signed (`codesign --force --sign -`). The engine source was never modified; nothing in
    the engine repo was touched.

    The point of the reword is that the new message contains NONE of the substrings
    `output::error_kind` triggers on, while the engine still classifies it `unsupported`. So a
    conductor that re-derives the kind from the wording answers `error` here and a conductor
    that relays the engine's answers `unsupported` — the two are distinguishable on this one
    capture and on nothing else the current engine emits.

    Rewording an error message is an ordinary, non-breaking thing to do in the engine, which is
    what makes deriving the kind from its prose the wrong contract.


SECOND BATCH — the two below. Same day, 2026-08-08, but a strictly later engine: a release build
at 0dd5997 ("fix(dupes): an apply emitted invalid JSON for a run that really deleted the file"),
also reporting burrow_cli 0.1.0. "Later" is the commit graph, not just the clock — e1b46b6 is an
ancestor of 0dd5997, and 5e42bf0 sits between them. The clock agrees: e1b46b6 committed 08:29,
first batch captured 10:28, 5e42bf0 committed 10:53, 0dd5997 committed 11:16, second batch
captured 11:35, all local time on 2026-08-08. So the first batch predates the platform guards and
the second postdates them, which is the only ordering under which both batches are what they say.
That second build is the one whose 5e42bf0 platform guards let
`engine::windows_refusal` be retired here, so these two exist to pin the consequence: `evict`
and `sentinel` are now SPAWNED on every platform instead of pre-empted, and whatever the engine
answers is what the caller gets.

Neither needed a sandbox or a patched binary. Each command has an honest failure it reaches on
macOS by itself, and a failure envelope for the RIGHT command is what the replay test needs —
replaying `net`'s refusal under `burrow evict` would prove the spawn but describe the wrong
command.


evict-error.json                                                                   (exit code 2)
    burrow-engine evict

    No path at all. `evict::parse` refuses, and the refusal is deliberately checked BEFORE the
    platform gate (`cli.rs:516`) so that malformed argv is called malformed on every platform —
    the engine's `evict.golden.provenance.txt` records that exact sentence as the oracle's answer
    and says an engine that accepts the no-arg form has diverged. Kind `error`, exit 2: the only
    capture here that does not exit 1, which is why `replaying_engine` takes the code.


sentinel-not-found.json                                                            (exit code 1)
    env -u HOME burrow-engine sentinel

    No positional, so the engine has to infer the trash directory, and `home_or_refuse` cannot
    tell it where home is. Kind `not_found` — a third classification, distinct from the
    `unsupported` and `error` already captured, so the relay is now exercised on every kind the
    engine actually emits.

    This is also the gate that sits ABOVE the off-macOS platform refusal in `cli.rs:2296`, and
    the ordering is deliberate on the engine's side: "I do not know where your home is" is the
    more specific answer, so it wins even on the platforms where the inferred `~/.Trash` would
    have been refused anyway.


WHAT IS NOT CAPTURED HERE, and cannot be from a macOS build: the off-macOS refusals themselves —
`sentinel`'s inferred-trash gate, `evict`'s platform gate, and the `dupes --apply` Windows guard.
Their predicates are `std::env::consts::OS` compared against a literal, so on a macOS host the
compiler folds every one of them to the served branch and dead-strips the refusal arms; none of
`"sentinel default trash"`, `"cloud-file dehydration needs macOS brctl"` or `"Windows duplicate
discovery is read-only"` appears anywhere in the release binary's bytes. There is no sandbox and
no same-length patch that can provoke code the linker removed. Those three are pinned in the
engine's own suite, which passes the OS in as an argument and therefore runs all three platforms'
answers on any host.
